chunks: Sa'd ibn Abdillah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Nu'man and Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Abdillah ibn Muskhan, who said: Aban al-Azraq narrated to me, from Zurarah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he said:

Whoever does not have the offering (hady) and wishes to fast the three days at the beginning of the ten [days of Dhul-Hijjah], there is no harm in that. This does not contradict the reports we have previously mentioned stating that the last of these three days is the Day of Arafah, because those reports are understood as referring to the preferred/virtuous act (fadl), while this report is understood as referring to the concession (rukhsah) for one who fears being unable to perform the offering. There is no contradiction between them on this basis.
ai.seo_question: How can fasting the first three days of Dhul-Hijjah coexist with the report that the last of those days is the Day of Arafah?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this narration from Abu Abdillah (Imam al-Sadiq) to clarify the ruling for pilgrims unable to afford the sacrificial offering (hady), permitting them to fast three days at the start of Dhul-Hijjah as a substitute. The scholar resolves the apparent tension with other reports by distinguishing between the superior virtue (fadl) of fasting on the Day of Arafah and the legal concession (rukhsah) for those lacking the means, demonstrating the nuanced interplay between obligation and flexibility in Shia jurisprudence.
